title: Improving Transformer Interpretability with Activation Contrast-Based Attribution

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to reveal why existing activation-based attribution methods have limited explanation quality. This is a specific empirical relationship that must be established in prior work to count as covered. None of the prior papers explicitly aim to reveal the limitations of activation-based attribution methods in terms of explanation quality. While some papers (e.g., [2], [4], [6], [14], [18], [23]) discuss issues with interpretability or limitations of specific attribution methods, none explicitly focus on the purpose of explaining why activation-based attribution methods specifically have limited explanation quality. Therefore, **purpose is not covered**.

### Mechanism
The contribution's mechanism involves analyzing activation information and observing that activation-based attribution methods may include class-irrelevant features in attribution maps, which reduces their quality. Paper [9] discusses the removal of class-irrelevant features in the context of few-shot image classification, and paper [17] introduces Class-Irrelevant Mapping (CIM) for few-shot classification, which also focuses on identifying and addressing class-irrelevant features. While these papers are in different domains, the underlying mechanism of identifying and addressing class-irrelevant features is substantively equivalent. Therefore, **mechanism is covered by [9] and [17]**.

### Evaluation
The contribution's evaluation involves qualitative observations and layer-wise heatmap comparisons (AttCAT vs. Contrast-CAT) as a motivation for the method. Paper [7] introduces the Contrastive Attributed explanations for Text (CAT) method and evaluates it using qualitative visualizations and comparisons of heatmaps. This evaluation design — qualitative heatmap comparisons — is substantively equivalent to the evaluation design in the contribution. Therefore, **evaluation is covered by [7]**.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of Transformer interpretability for text classification. Several prior papers ([2], [6], [7], [22]) address Transformer interpretability in the context of text classification or related tasks. For example, [2] discusses improving attention-based interpretability for text classification, and [7] focuses on contrastive explanations for text data. These papers establish that the domain of Transformer interpretability for text classification is not new. Therefore, **domain is covered by [2], [6], [7], and [22]**.

**PURPOSE: 生成更清晰、更忠实的 token 级归因图**

The purpose is to produce cleaner, more faithful token-level attribution maps for Transformer models. Paper [14] (AttCAT) explicitly aims to explain Transformers via token-level attribution, criticizing existing methods for lacking faithfulness. Paper [28] (GlobEnc) also aims at "quantifying global token attribution" in Transformers with improved accuracy. Paper [10] (DecompX) explains Transformer decisions by propagating token decomposition. All three share the same objective: improve faithfulness/clarity of token-level attribution in Transformers. Paper [14] is the closest match — "do not necessarily provide a faithful explanation" and proposes attentive class activation tokens as a remedy.

---

**MECHANISM: 激活对比框架 — 用目标激活与多个不同类别参考激活之差过滤类别无关特征，再结合梯度信息构造 token 级归因图**

The core primitive is: (1) subtract reference-class activations from target-class activations to cancel class-agnostic features, then (2) combine with gradients to form attribution maps. 

- Paper [14] (AttCAT) combines attention weights with feature magnitudes (gradient-like signals) for token attribution — but does NOT use contrastive activation subtraction across classes.
- Paper [25] (Counterfactual-based Saliency Map) addresses "Why P rather than Q?" contrastive explanations using counterfactual inputs, but operates on input space, not internal activation contrasting.
- Paper [32] addresses noisy saliency maps by analyzing irrelevant features through ReLU — related but not the same primitive.
- Paper [30] analyzes baseline signal choice in XAI attribution methods — closest to the "reference activation" idea, but focuses on input baselines (like Integrated Gradients), not cross-class activation subtraction.
- Paper [6] (Novel CAM) uses "positive and negative regions" for CAM weighting — this is somewhat related (using negative/other-class information), but in the image/CAM domain and not the same activation-contrasting primitive.
- Paper [17] (Causal CAM) uses causal reasoning for CAM in segmentation — different mechanism.
- Paper [5] (Contrast-Consistent Search adapted to multiclass) — the title suggests contrast-based methods for classification, potentially relevant, but the abstract is not provided; CCS is about finding linear probes via contrast pairs, not activation-contrasting for attribution maps.

No prior paper presents the specific primitive of subtracting multi-class reference activations from target activations to filter class-agnostic features, then combining with gradients for token-level attribution in Transformers. The closest analogues (contrastive explanations, baseline-dependent attribution) differ in the specific primitive.

**EVALUATION: 消融对比 'Random' 与 'Same' 版本，论证不同类别激活作对比参考是关键**

The evaluation design involves: (a) quantitative results on a benchmark (C3), and (b) ablation comparing variants (Random reference vs. Same-class reference vs. Different-class reference). The ablation design — swapping the reference type and measuring attribution quality — is a standard component substitution/ablation experiment. Papers [14], [28], [10] all include ablation studies comparing variants of their attribution methods on standard NLP benchmarks. The design of "swap a component (reference type), measure attribution faithfulness" is a generic ablation shape present in many prior papers. However, per the special rule, generic ablation shapes don't establish coverage unless they validate the same claim. The specific claim (different-class reference is key) is unique. But the evaluation DESIGN (quantitative benchmark + component ablation) is standard and appears in [14] and [28]. Per the rules, the design (ablation + standard benchmark metrics) is covered.

Papers [14], [28], [10], [1], [8] all work in Transformer interpretability/explainability for NLP/text classification. This domain is clearly covered.
